[Textbook misprint: this question prints only THREE alternatives, (a) to (c) — there is no (d) — and two of the three are genuine fusion reactions. Both (a) and (b) appear in this chapter's own list of the fusion reactions of the Sun and stars (section 13.7.5, reactions (i) and (ii)). Only (c) is not a fusion reaction. The question therefore has no single correct answer, and it is presented here as a free-response question with the three printed alternatives in the stem rather than as a multiple-choice question with an invented fourth option.]

Section 13.7.5 defines nuclear fusion as the process in which lighter nuclei combine (fuse) together to form a heavier nucleus, with the release of an enormous amount of energy.

**Choice (c) is not a fusion reaction.** \(^{3}_{1}\mathrm{H} + {}^{1}_{1}\mathrm{H} \longrightarrow {}^{3}_{1}\mathrm{H} + {}^{1}_{1}\mathrm{p}\) has \(^{3}_{1}\mathrm{H}\) on both sides and a proton \(^{1}_{1}\mathrm{p}\), which is the same particle as the \(^{1}_{1}\mathrm{H}\) it started with. Nothing has combined and no heavier nucleus has been formed, so this is not fusion.

**Choice (b) IS a fusion reaction.** \(^{2}_{1}\mathrm{H} + {}^{1}_{1}\mathrm{H} \longrightarrow {}^{3}_{2}\mathrm{He}\) balances in both mass number (\(2 + 1 = 3\)) and atomic number (\(1 + 1 = 2\)), and two light nuclei have united into a single heavier one. This is exactly reaction (ii) of the list of fusion reactions of the Sun and stars printed in section 13.7.5.

**Choice (a) is ALSO a fusion reaction.** \(^{1}_{1}\mathrm{H} + {}^{1}_{1}\mathrm{H} \longrightarrow {}^{2}_{1}\mathrm{H} + {}^{0}_{1}\mathrm{e}\) balances in mass number (\(2 = 2 + 0\)) and, with \(^{0}_{1}\mathrm{e}\) read as a positron, in atomic number too (\(2 = 1 + 1\)). Two hydrogen nuclei have fused into a deuterium nucleus, and this is reaction (i) of the same printed list.

So the choices as printed contain **two** correct answers, (a) and (b), and no fourth choice is printed at all. A student who answers either is right.

The nuclides with an **even number of protons and an even number of neutrons** are the most stable.

Table 13.2 counts the naturally occurring nuclides by the even/odd character of \(Z\) and \(N\):

| \(Z\) | \(N\) | number of such nuclides |
|---|---|---|
| Even | Even | 165 |
| Even | Odd | 55 |
| Odd | Even | 50 |
| Odd | Odd | 4 |

The even-even nuclides are by far the largest group, and they make up about 85 % of the earth's crust. The reason given in the chapter is that nucleons pair up: in an even-even nuclide every proton has a proton partner and every neutron a neutron partner, and this proton-proton and neutron-neutron pairing imparts stability to the nucleus.

**Nuclear fission** (section 13.7.3) is the splitting of the heavy nucleus of an atom into two nearly equal fragments, accompanied by the release of a large amount of energy.

When a uranium nucleus absorbs a neutron it breaks up, releasing energy as heat, more neutrons and other radiation. The example given in the chapter is

\(^{235}_{92}\mathrm{U} + {}^{1}_{0}\mathrm{n} \longrightarrow {}^{142}_{56}\mathrm{Ba} + {}^{91}_{36}\mathrm{Kr} + 3\ {}^{1}_{0}\mathrm{n} + \text{Energy}\)

Points to note:

- The total mass of the fission products is less than that of the parent nucleus, and the energy released corresponds to that mass loss. The energy released per fission is about 200 MeV.
- There is no unique way for \(^{235}\mathrm{U}\) to split: about 400 modes of fission leading to some 800 fission products are known, and many of these products are themselves radioactive.
- Each fission emits 2 to 3 neutrons (2.5 on average). These neutrons cause further fissions, which release still more neutrons, so the process can continue by itself as a **chain reaction** even after the bombarding neutrons are removed.

Stability comes from the pairing of nucleons, and the chapter states that this pairing takes place **separately** between protons and between neutrons — a proton does not pair with a neutron.

In a nuclide with an odd number of protons AND an odd number of neutrons, one proton is left without a proton partner and one neutron is left without a neutron partner. The nucleus therefore carries **two unpaired nucleons**, which is the largest number possible, and gets the least benefit from pairing.

The evidence given in the chapter is the count itself: of the naturally occurring nuclides only **four** are odd-odd (Table 13.2), against 165 that are even-even, and these odd-odd nuclides make up only about 2 % of the earth's crust. So small a number is itself an indication of instability.

Figure 13.1 plots the neutron number \(N\) against the proton number \(Z\) for the stable nuclides. They fall inside a band called the **stability zone (stability belt)**; any nuclide formed outside the belt is radioactive, and it decays in whichever way moves it back towards the belt.

**Nuclides lying ABOVE the belt are \(\beta^{-}\) emitters.** These have too many neutrons for their number of protons, that is an \(N/Z\) ratio higher than the belt allows. In \(\beta^{-}\) decay (section 13.6.2)

\(^{A}_{Z}\mathrm{X} \longrightarrow {}^{A}_{Z+1}\mathrm{Y} + {}^{0}_{-1}\mathrm{e}\)

the mass number is unchanged while the atomic number rises by one — in effect a neutron is replaced by a proton. That lowers \(N/Z\) and brings the nuclide down into the belt.

**Nuclides lying BELOW the belt are \(\beta^{+}\) (positron) emitters.** These have too few neutrons, that is an \(N/Z\) ratio lower than the belt allows. Positron emission does the reverse: the chapter's example in section 13.7.2 is

\(^{13}_{7}\mathrm{N} \longrightarrow {}^{13}_{6}\mathrm{C} + {}^{0}_{1}\mathrm{e}\)

where the mass number is again unchanged but the atomic number FALLS by one — a proton is replaced by a neutron. That raises \(N/Z\) and lifts the nuclide up into the belt.

[Note: the chapter states the stability belt, \(\beta^{-}\) decay and positron emission in three separate places (13.3.2, 13.6.2 and 13.7.2); Fig. 13.1 itself is not labelled with the two emitter regions, so the answer above is obtained by combining those three statements.]

**Nuclear transmutation** (section 13.7.1) is the transformation of a stable nucleus into another nucleus, whether the product is stable or unstable. It is a non-spontaneous, man-made nuclear reaction. Example:

\(^{10}_{5}\mathrm{B} + {}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He} \longrightarrow {}^{13}_{7}\mathrm{N} + {}^{1}_{0}\mathrm{n}\)

Here the stable nuclide \(^{10}_{5}\mathrm{B}\) has been converted into a different element by bombardment with \(\alpha\)-particles.

**Artificial (induced) radioactivity** (section 13.7.2) is that particular kind of transmutation in which the PRODUCT nucleus is radioactive, so that it goes on to decay spontaneously with emission of radiation and particles. In the same example the product \(^{13}_{7}\mathrm{N}\) is unstable and decays by emitting a positron:

\(^{13}_{7}\mathrm{N} \longrightarrow {}^{13}_{6}\mathrm{C} + {}^{0}_{1}\mathrm{e}\)

**The difference:** transmutation is the general process — it only requires that one nucleus be turned into another, and the product may be perfectly stable. Artificial radioactivity is the special case of transmutation in which the product is radioactive. Every case of artificial radioactivity is a transmutation, but not every transmutation produces artificial radioactivity.

**Binding energy per nucleon** is the total nuclear binding energy of a nuclide divided by the number of nucleons it contains:

\(\overline{B} = \dfrac{\mathrm{B.E.}}{A}\)

where the total binding energy is obtained from the mass defect, \(\mathrm{B.E.} = \Delta m\ (\mathrm{u}) \times 931.4\) MeV. It measures how strongly, on average, each nucleon is held inside the nucleus, so it is the proper basis for comparing nuclei of different sizes.

**The diagram (Fig. 13.2)** is a plot of \(\overline{B}\) (in MeV) on the vertical axis against the mass number \(A\) on the horizontal axis, for the most stable isotope of each mass number. The curve rises steeply from very small \(A\), reaches a broad maximum near \(A \approx 56\), and then falls away slowly towards the heavy end. **The higher a nuclide sits on this curve, the more stable it is.** The chapter draws three inferences from it:

- **Light nuclides, \(A < 30\):** the curve is low but shows sharp peaks at mass numbers that are multiples of 4 — \(^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}\), \(^{12}_{6}\mathrm{C}\), \(^{16}_{8}\mathrm{O}\) are noticeably more stable than their neighbours.
- **Medium-mass nuclides, \(30 < A < 90\):** \(\overline{B}\) rises from about 8 MeV at \(A = 16\) to about 8.3 MeV for \(A\) between 28 and 32, stays near 8.5 MeV, and then passes through a broad maximum. The nuclides on that maximum are the most stable of all; \(^{56}\mathrm{Fe}\), with \(\overline{B} = 8.79\) MeV, is the most stable nuclide.
- **Heavy nuclides, \(A > 90\):** \(\overline{B}\) falls from the maximum of 8.79 MeV to about 7.7 MeV at \(A \approx 210\). \(^{209}\mathrm{Bi}\) is the heaviest stable nuclide; beyond it every nuclide is radioactive and an \(\alpha\)-emitter.

The two arms of the curve are also what make fusion and fission release energy: light nuclei move UP the rising arm when they fuse, and heavy nuclei move UP the falling arm when they split, and in both cases the gain in \(\overline{B}\) appears as released energy.

**\(\alpha\)-decay** (section 13.6.1) is the emission of an \(\alpha\)-particle from a nucleus. An \(\alpha\)-particle carries a charge of \(+2\) and has a mass of 4 u; it is identical with the helium nucleus and is written \(^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}\).

When a parent nucleus emits an \(\alpha\)-particle it loses two protons and two neutrons, so the daughter nucleus has a mass number 4 units smaller and an atomic number 2 units smaller. The general equation is

\(^{A}_{Z}\mathrm{X} \longrightarrow {}^{A-4}_{Z-2}\mathrm{Y} + {}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}\)

**Example** — radium-226 decays to radon-222:

\(^{226}_{88}\mathrm{Ra} \longrightarrow {}^{222}_{86}\mathrm{Rn} + {}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}\)

A second example given in the chapter is uranium-238 decaying to thorium-234:

\(^{238}_{92}\mathrm{U} \longrightarrow {}^{234}_{90}\mathrm{Th} + {}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}\)

Because the atomic number falls by 2, the daughter element occupies a place two positions to the left of the parent in the periodic table.

Section 13.7.5 states the advantage and the obstacle together.

**The advantage:** fusion produces relatively more energy per given mass of fuel than fission does.

**The difficulty:** fusion requires an extremely high temperature, typically of the order of \(10^{8}\) K.

The reason such a temperature is needed is that the nuclei which must fuse are all positively charged, and section 13.3.4 has already established that the Coulomb repulsion between two positive charges at nuclear separations is very large. The short-range nuclear attractive forces only take over once the nuclei are already within about \(10^{-15}\) m of each other, so the nuclei must be thrown together with enormous kinetic energy to get that close — and it is temperature that supplies that kinetic energy.

That is why fusion is not yet a practical energy source: no ordinary container can hold matter at \(10^{8}\) K, whereas a fission chain reaction proceeds with slow neutrons at ordinary reactor temperatures and can simply be moderated and controlled with cadmium rods.

The \(N/Z\) ratio is the single most useful indicator of whether a nuclide is stable, and section 13.3.2 develops it from **Fig. 13.1**.

**The diagram.** Fig. 13.1 plots the number of neutrons \(N\) (vertical axis, 0 to about 150) against the number of protons \(Z\) (horizontal axis, 0 to 100). Each stable nuclide is one point. The straight line \(N = Z\) is drawn through the plot. Because most elements have several stable isotopes, the points do not lie on a single curve but form a band — the **stability zone** or **stability belt**. All stable nuclides fall inside this belt; anything formed outside it is radioactive.

**What the diagram shows.**

- For the light nuclides, up to about \(^{40}_{20}\mathrm{Ca}\), the straight line \(N = Z\) passes right through the belt. So light nuclides are stable when \(N/Z\) is nearly 1 — they need about as many neutrons as protons.
- Beyond calcium the belt bends away above the \(N = Z\) line and becomes curved, with \(N/Z\) increasing steadily to values greater than 1. Heavier nuclides therefore need MORE neutrons than protons in order to be stable.
- The reason the chapter gives is Coulomb repulsion: a heavier nuclide has a larger number of protons and hence a large repulsion between them. Adding extra neutrons separates the protons further from one another, which reduces that repulsion and renders the nucleus stable.

So a nuclide whose \(N/Z\) places it inside the belt is stable, and one whose \(N/Z\) is too high or too low for its \(Z\) lies outside the belt and is radioactive.

The age of an old wood sample is found by **radiocarbon dating** (section 13.8.1). The method rests on the following chain of facts.

i. Radioactive \(^{14}\mathrm{C}\) is continuously formed in the upper atmosphere by the bombardment of \(^{14}\mathrm{N}\) with neutrons from cosmic rays:

\(^{14}_{7}\mathrm{N} + {}^{1}_{0}\mathrm{n} \longrightarrow {}^{14}_{6}\mathrm{C} + {}^{1}_{1}\mathrm{H}\)

ii. This \(^{14}\mathrm{C}\) combines with atmospheric oxygen to give \(^{14}\mathrm{CO_2}\), which mixes with ordinary \(^{12}\mathrm{CO_2}\).

iii. Plants absorb the carbon dioxide during photosynthesis and animals eat plants, so \(^{14}\mathrm{C}\) becomes part of every living plant and animal body.

iv. As long as the tree is alive the ratio \(^{14}\mathrm{C}/^{12}\mathrm{C}\) in it stays constant. Once the tree dies photosynthesis stops, no fresh \(^{14}\mathrm{C}\) is taken in, and the ratio falls as the \(^{14}\mathrm{C}\) already present decays (half life 5730 years):

\(^{14}_{6}\mathrm{C} \longrightarrow {}^{14}_{7}\mathrm{N} + {}^{0}_{-1}\mathrm{e}\)

v. **The measurement.** Measure the activity \(N\) of the given wood sample and the activity \(N_0\) of a fresh sample from a living plant. \(N_0\) is what the given sample's activity was at the moment of its death.

vi. **The calculation.** The period for which the sample has been dead is then

\(t = \dfrac{2.303}{\lambda}\ \log_{10}\dfrac{N_0}{N}\), where \(\lambda = \dfrac{0.693}{5730\ \mathrm{y}} = 1.21 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{y^{-1}}\)

**Mirror nuclei** are isobars in which the numbers of protons and neutrons differ by 1 and are interchanged between the two members of the pair.

The two examples given in section 13.2.1 are:

- \(^{3}_{1}\mathrm{H}\) and \(^{3}_{2}\mathrm{He}\) — the first has \(Z = 1\), \(N = 2\); the second has \(Z = 2\), \(N = 1\).
- \(^{13}_{6}\mathrm{C}\) and \(^{13}_{7}\mathrm{N}\) — the first has \(Z = 6\), \(N = 7\); the second has \(Z = 7\), \(N = 6\).

In each pair the mass number is the same (so they are isobars), and the proton and neutron counts of one member are exactly the neutron and proton counts of the other.

[Textbook misprint: the product iodine nuclide is printed with the numbers after the symbol and with the subscript 54, the same atomic number as the xenon it comes from. Read literally the missing particle would have \(A = 0\) and \(Z = 0\), that is nothing at all. The atomic number of iodine is 53, so the product is \(^{118}_{53}\mathrm{I}\), and the answer below uses that value.]

The missing particle is a **positron**, \(^{0}_{1}\mathrm{e}\), and the balanced reaction is

\(^{118}_{54}\mathrm{Xe} \longrightarrow {}^{0}_{1}\mathrm{e} + {}^{118}_{53}\mathrm{I}\)

**How it is obtained.** Iodine has atomic number 53, so the product nuclide is \(^{118}_{53}\mathrm{I}\). Balancing then gives:

- mass number: \(118 = 0 + 118\), so the missing particle has \(A = 0\);
- atomic number: \(54 = Z + 53\), so the missing particle has \(Z = +1\).

A particle of zero mass number and charge \(+1\) is the positron. The chapter uses exactly this particle in section 13.7.2, where \(^{13}_{7}\mathrm{N} \longrightarrow {}^{13}_{6}\mathrm{C} + {}^{0}_{1}\mathrm{e}\). This is consistent with the \(N/Z\) argument of section 13.3.2: \(^{118}_{54}\mathrm{Xe}\) has \(N/Z = 64/54 = 1.19\), which is low for a nuclide of this mass, so it lies below the stability belt and corrects itself by converting a proton into a neutron.

The most stable nuclide known is **\(^{56}\mathrm{Fe}\)** (iron-56), which the chapter names in its discussion of Fig. 13.2.

Two factors responsible for its stability:

1. **It has the highest binding energy per nucleon of any nuclide.** \(^{56}\mathrm{Fe}\) sits on the broad maximum of the plot of \(\overline{B}\) against mass number, with \(\overline{B} = 8.79\) MeV. Since \(\overline{B}\) measures how strongly each nucleon is held, no nuclide holds its nucleons more tightly.

2. **It is an even-even nuclide.** Iron-56 has \(Z = 26\) protons and \(N = 56 - 26 = 30\) neutrons, both even. By section 13.3.1 every proton and every neutron therefore has a partner of its own kind, and this proton-proton and neutron-neutron pairing is what makes even-even nuclides the most stable class — they are 165 of the naturally occurring nuclides and about 85 % of the earth's crust.

(Its neutron-to-proton ratio, \(N/Z = 30/26 = 1.15\), also places it comfortably inside the stability belt of Fig. 13.1.)

The decay constant \(\lambda\) and the half life \(t_{1/2}\) of a radioelement are related by

\(\lambda = \dfrac{0.693}{t_{1/2}}\)  or equivalently  \(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{\lambda}\)

The two are therefore **inversely proportional**: the shorter the half life, the larger the decay constant, and their product is always 0.693 (which is \(\ln 2\)). Note also that the relation contains no reference to \(N_0\) — the half life of a radioelement does not depend on how much of it you start with.

An \(\alpha\)-particle is a helium **nucleus**; a helium **atom** is that nucleus together with its two electrons.

Section 13.6.1 states that the \(\alpha\)-particle carries a charge of \(+2\) and has a mass of 4 u, and that it is identical with the helium nucleus, which is why it is written \(^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}\).

The differences that follow are:

- **Charge.** An \(\alpha\)-particle carries a net charge of \(+2\) (it is \(\mathrm{He^{2+}}\)); a helium atom is electrically neutral, because its \(+2\) nuclear charge is exactly cancelled by its two electrons.
- **Electrons.** An \(\alpha\)-particle has no electrons at all; a helium atom has two.
- **Mass.** Their masses are very nearly the same, because the mass of an electron is negligible — about \(1/1837\) of the mass of a proton — so both are close to 4 u.

One point of difference, taken from Table 13.3: **a chemical reaction is only a rearrangement of atoms, brought about by the breaking and forming of chemical bonds, so every element present at the start is still present at the end; a nuclear reaction converts one element or isotope into another element altogether.**

The table lists four further points, any one of which would also answer the question:

| Chemical reactions | Nuclear reactions |
|---|---|
| Different isotopes of an element behave the same. | Isotopes of an element behave differently. |
| Only the outer-shell electrons take part. | Protons, neutrons and other elementary particles take part as well as electrons. |
| Relatively small energy changes — burning 1.0 g of methane releases only 56 kJ. | Very large energy changes — the nuclear transformation of 1 g of uranium-235 releases \(8.2 \times 10^{7}\) kJ. |
| The rate is influenced by temperature, pressure, concentration and catalyst. | The rate is unaffected by temperature, pressure and catalyst. |

[Textbook misprint, two places. (i) The fifth nuclide is printed as \(^{28}_{14}\mathrm{S}\): — the element of atomic number 14 is silicon, so the trailing colon is the letter i and the nuclide is \(^{28}_{14}\mathrm{Si}\). (ii) As the five nuclides are printed, no two of them share a mass number, so the list contains NO pair of mirror nuclei and that half of the question cannot be answered. Reading the first entry as \(^{11}_{5}\mathrm{B}\) rather than \(^{10}_{5}\mathrm{B}\) makes it and \(^{11}_{6}\mathrm{C}\) a mirror pair and leaves two clean isotone pairs, which is very probably what was intended.]

First find \(N = A - Z\) for each of the five nuclides:

| nuclide | \(Z\) | \(A\) | \(N = A - Z\) |
|---|---|---|---|
| \(^{10}_{5}\mathrm{B}\) | 5 | 10 | 5 |
| \(^{12}_{6}\mathrm{C}\) | 6 | 12 | 6 |
| \(^{27}_{13}\mathrm{Al}\) | 13 | 27 | 14 |
| \(^{11}_{6}\mathrm{C}\) | 6 | 11 | 5 |
| \(^{28}_{14}\mathrm{Si}\) | 14 | 28 | 14 |

**Isotones** are nuclides with the same number of neutrons but different numbers of protons. Reading the last column, the pairs are

- \(^{10}_{5}\mathrm{B}\) and \(^{11}_{6}\mathrm{C}\) — both have \(N = 5\);
- \(^{27}_{13}\mathrm{Al}\) and \(^{28}_{14}\mathrm{Si}\) — both have \(N = 14\).

**Mirror nuclei** are isobars (same mass number) in which the proton and neutron counts are interchanged. **No two of the five nuclides as printed share a mass number**, so as the list stands it contains no mirror pair. If the first entry is read as \(^{11}_{5}\mathrm{B}\) (\(Z = 5\), \(N = 6\)), then it and \(^{11}_{6}\mathrm{C}\) (\(Z = 6\), \(N = 5\)) are a mirror pair, and the isotone pairs become \(^{11}_{5}\mathrm{B}\) with \(^{12}_{6}\mathrm{C}\) (both \(N = 6\)) and \(^{27}_{13}\mathrm{Al}\) with \(^{28}_{14}\mathrm{Si}\).

Start from the integrated rate law for radioactive decay, Eq. (13.9) of section 13.5.3:

\(\lambda = \dfrac{2.303}{t}\ \log_{10}\dfrac{N_0}{N}\)

where \(N_0\) is the number of nuclei at \(t = 0\) and \(N\) the number remaining at time \(t\).

**Apply the definition of half life.** The half life \(t_{1/2}\) is the time needed for the nuclei to decay to exactly half their initial value, so at \(t = t_{1/2}\) we have \(N = N_0/2\). Substituting:

\(\lambda = \dfrac{2.303}{t_{1/2}}\ \log_{10}\dfrac{N_0}{N_0/2}\)

\(= \dfrac{2.303}{t_{1/2}}\ \log_{10} 2\)

\(= \dfrac{2.303}{t_{1/2}} \times 0.3010\)

\(= \dfrac{0.693}{t_{1/2}}\)

**Hence**

\(\lambda = \dfrac{0.693}{t_{1/2}}\)  and  \(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{\lambda}\)

Notice that \(N_0\) cancelled out of the ratio, so the half life is independent of the amount of radioelement taken.

**The relation to be plotted.** Taking logarithms to base 10 of Eq. (13.9) gives

\(\log_{10} N = -\dfrac{\lambda}{2.303}\ t + \log_{10} N_0\)

The rate of decay (the activity) is proportional to \(N\), so replacing \(N\) by the activity changes only the intercept and not the gradient:

\(\log_{10}(\text{activity}) = -\dfrac{\lambda}{2.303}\ t + \text{constant}\)

**The graph (Fig. 13.3).** This is of the form \(y = mx + c\), so a plot of \(\log_{10}\)(activity / dps) on the vertical axis against \(t/\mathrm{s}\) on the horizontal axis is a **straight line sloping downwards**, starting at the intercept \(\log_{10}\)(initial activity) on the vertical axis and falling steadily as \(t\) increases.

**The slope** is

\(\text{slope} = -\dfrac{\lambda}{2.303}\)

It is negative because the activity decreases with time. Measuring the slope of such a plot is the standard way of obtaining the decay constant: \(\lambda = -2.303 \times \text{slope}\), and hence \(t_{1/2} = 0.693/\lambda\).

The two units of radioactivity given in section 13.5.6 are the **curie (Ci)** and the **becquerel (Bq)**.

- **Becquerel:** \(1\ \mathrm{Bq} = 1\) disintegration per second (dps). This is the SI unit and is the smaller of the two.
- **Curie:** \(1\ \mathrm{Ci} = 3.7 \times 10^{10}\) dps.

**How they are interrelated:** since both are counts of disintegrations per second,

\(1\ \mathrm{Ci} = 3.7 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{dps} = 3.7 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{Bq}\)

Equivalently, \(1\ \mathrm{Bq} = 2.7 \times 10^{-11}\ \mathrm{Ci}\).

Given: \(t_{1/2} = 900\) minutes.

Using \(\lambda = \dfrac{0.693}{t_{1/2}}\),

\(\lambda = \dfrac{0.693}{900\ \mathrm{min}} = 7.70 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}\)

**The decay constant of \(^{24}\mathrm{Na}\) is \(7.70 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}\).**

(In seconds this is \(7.70 \times 10^{-4} / 60 = 1.28 \times 10^{-5}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}\). Note that \(\lambda\) always carries the reciprocal of whatever time unit the half life was quoted in.)

Given: \(\lambda = 0.017\ \mathrm{h^{-1}}\).

Using \(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{\lambda}\),

\(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{0.017\ \mathrm{h^{-1}}} = 40.76\ \mathrm{h}\)

**The half life of \(^{197}\mathrm{Hg}\) is 40.76 hours** (about 1.7 days).

Given: total binding energy of \(^{58}\mathrm{Ni}\) = 508 MeV, and its mass number \(A = 58\).

Using Eq. (13.4), \(\overline{B} = \dfrac{\mathrm{B.E.}}{A}\),

\(\overline{B} = \dfrac{508\ \mathrm{MeV}}{58} = 8.76\ \mathrm{MeV\ per\ nucleon}\)

**The binding energy per nucleon of \(^{58}\mathrm{Ni}\) is 8.76 MeV.**

This value is close to the maximum of the binding-energy curve (8.79 MeV for \(^{56}\mathrm{Fe}\)), which is consistent with nickel-58 being a very stable nuclide lying near the peak of Fig. 13.2.

For \(^{32}_{16}\mathrm{S}\): \(Z = 16\), \(A = 32\), so the number of neutrons is \(A - Z = 32 - 16 = 16\).

Using Eq. (13.2), \(\Delta m = [Z m_{\mathrm{H}} + (A - Z) m_{\mathrm{n}}] - m\):

\(\Delta m = [16 \times 1.0078\ \mathrm{u} + 16 \times 1.0087\ \mathrm{u}] - 31.97\ \mathrm{u}\)

\(= [16.1248 + 16.1392]\ \mathrm{u} - 31.97\ \mathrm{u}\)

\(= 32.2640\ \mathrm{u} - 31.97\ \mathrm{u}\)

\(= 0.294\ \mathrm{u}\)

**The mass defect of \(^{32}_{16}\mathrm{S}\) is 0.294 u.**

(For interest, the corresponding binding energy is \(0.294 \times 931.4 = 273.8\) MeV, or 8.56 MeV per nucleon.)

[Textbook misprint: the first of the four fusion reactions printed in section 13.7.5 is given as \(^{1}_{1}\mathrm{H} + {}^{1}_{1}\mathrm{H} \longrightarrow {}^{2}_{1}\mathrm{H} + {}^{0}_{-1}\mathrm{e}\), which does not balance in charge — the left-hand side carries \(+2\) and the right-hand side \(1 - 1 = 0\). The emitted particle is a positron, \(^{0}_{1}\mathrm{e}\), which makes both sides \(+2\); the same reaction is printed with the positron in exercise 1 (A) of this chapter. The answer below gives the balanced form.]

Section 13.7.5 gives four representative fusion reactions occurring in the Sun and stars:

i. \(^{1}_{1}\mathrm{H} + {}^{1}_{1}\mathrm{H} \longrightarrow {}^{2}_{1}\mathrm{H} + {}^{0}_{1}\mathrm{e}\)

ii. \(^{1}_{1}\mathrm{H} + {}^{2}_{1}\mathrm{H} \longrightarrow {}^{3}_{2}\mathrm{He}\)

iii. \(^{3}_{2}\mathrm{He} + {}^{3}_{2}\mathrm{He} \longrightarrow {}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He} + 2\ {}^{1}_{1}\mathrm{H}\)

iv. \(^{3}_{2}\mathrm{He} + {}^{1}_{1}\mathrm{H} \longrightarrow {}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He} + {}^{0}_{1}\mathrm{e}\)

In every one of these, light nuclei combine to form a heavier nucleus, and the energy the earth receives from the Sun is the result. Such reactions need a temperature of the order of \(10^{8}\) K, which is available in the interior of a star.

**Step 1 — count the \(\alpha\)-particles from the mass number.** Only \(\alpha\)-emission changes the mass number, and each \(\alpha\)-particle removes 4 units. \(\beta\)-emission leaves the mass number unchanged.

Net decrease in mass number \(= 232 - 208 = 24\)

Number of \(\alpha\)-particles \(= \dfrac{24}{4} = 6\)

**Step 2 — count the \(\beta\)-particles from the atomic number.** Each \(\alpha\)-particle lowers the atomic number by 2, and each \(\beta\)-particle raises it by 1.

The 6 \(\alpha\)-particles alone would lower the atomic number by \(6 \times 2 = 12\), taking it from 90 to 78.

The actual atomic number of the product is 82, which is 4 higher than 78. That increase of 4 can only come from \(\beta\)-emission, so

Number of \(\beta\)-particles \(= 4\)

**Check:** \(A: 232 - 6 \times 4 = 208\ \checkmark\);  \(Z: 90 - 6 \times 2 + 4 \times 1 = 90 - 12 + 4 = 82\ \checkmark\)

**6 \(\alpha\)-particles and 4 \(\beta\)-particles are emitted.**

Section 13.6.1 states that in \(\alpha\)-decay the atomic number falls by 2, so **the daughter element occupies a place two positions to the LEFT of the parent in the periodic table.**

Here B is the daughter and A is the parent. B lies two places to the left of A, so A lies **two places to the right of B**.

B is in group 16, therefore A is in group \(16 + 2 = 18\).

**A belongs to group 18** (the noble gases). This is consistent with the chapter's own example of \(\alpha\)-decay: \(^{226}_{88}\mathrm{Ra} \longrightarrow {}^{222}_{86}\mathrm{Rn} + {}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}\), where radium in group 2 gives radon in group 18, again a shift of two places.

**Step 1 — count the \(\alpha\)-particles from the mass number.** Only \(\alpha\)-emission changes the mass number, each \(\alpha\)-particle removing 4 units.

Net decrease in mass number \(= 222 - 214 = 8\)

Number of \(\alpha\)-particles \(= \dfrac{8}{4} = 2\)

**Step 2 — count the \(\beta\)-particles from the atomic number.**

The 2 \(\alpha\)-particles alone would lower the atomic number by \(2 \times 2 = 4\), taking it from 86 to 82.

The actual atomic number of the product is 84, which is 2 higher than 82. Since each \(\beta\)-particle raises the atomic number by 1,

Number of \(\beta\)-particles \(= 2\)

**Check:** \(A: 222 - 2 \times 4 = 214\ \checkmark\);  \(Z: 86 - 2 \times 2 + 2 \times 1 = 86 - 4 + 2 = 84\ \checkmark\)

**2 \(\alpha\)-particles and 2 \(\beta\)-particles are emitted.**

Given: \(t_{1/2} = 110\) min, \(t = 20\) min.

**Step 1 — decay constant.**

\(\lambda = \dfrac{0.693}{t_{1/2}} = \dfrac{0.693}{110\ \mathrm{min}} = 6.30 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}\)

**Step 2 — fraction remaining.** From Eq. (13.9), \(\log_{10}\dfrac{N_0}{N} = \dfrac{\lambda t}{2.303}\):

\(\log_{10}\dfrac{N_0}{N} = \dfrac{6.30 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{min^{-1}} \times 20\ \mathrm{min}}{2.303} = \dfrac{0.126}{2.303} = 0.0547\)

\(\dfrac{N_0}{N} = \mathrm{antilog}\ (0.0547) = 1.1343\)

\(\dfrac{N}{N_0} = \dfrac{1}{1.1343} = 0.8816\)

**Step 3 — fraction decayed.**

fraction decayed \(= 1 - \dfrac{N}{N_0} = 1 - 0.8816 = 0.118\)

**About 0.118, that is 11.8 %, of the \(^{18}\mathrm{F}\) sample decays in 20 minutes.** (The answer is a fraction and so has no unit.)

Given: \(t_{1/2} = 87.8\) d, \(t = 180\) d. Take \(N_0 = 100\).

**Step 1 — decay constant.**

\(\lambda = \dfrac{0.693}{87.8\ \mathrm{d}} = 7.893 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{d^{-1}}\)

**Step 2 — apply the rate law.**

\(\log_{10}\dfrac{N_0}{N} = \dfrac{\lambda t}{2.303} = \dfrac{7.893 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{d^{-1}} \times 180\ \mathrm{d}}{2.303} = \dfrac{1.4207}{2.303} = 0.6169\)

\(\dfrac{N_0}{N} = \mathrm{antilog}\ (0.6169) = 4.139\)

**Step 3 — percentage remaining.**

\(N = \dfrac{100}{4.139} = 24.2\)

**24.2 % of the \(^{35}\mathrm{S}\) sample remains after 180 days.**

(As a check, 180 d is a little over two half lives, and two half lives would leave 25 %.)

Given: \(t_{1/2} = 78\) h. 12 % of the sample decays, so 88 % remains: take \(N_0 = 100\) and \(N = 88\).

**Step 1 — decay constant.**

\(\lambda = \dfrac{0.693}{78\ \mathrm{h}} = 8.885 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{h^{-1}}\)

**Step 2 — apply the rate law.** From \(\lambda = \dfrac{2.303}{t}\ \log_{10}\dfrac{N_0}{N}\),

\(t = \dfrac{2.303}{\lambda}\ \log_{10}\dfrac{100}{88} = \dfrac{2.303}{8.885 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{h^{-1}}} \times \log_{10}(1.1364)\)

\(= 259.2\ \mathrm{h} \times 0.05552 = 14.4\ \mathrm{h}\)

**It takes about 14.4 hours for 12 % of the \(^{67}\mathrm{Ga}\) sample to decay.**

(The unit is hours, since the half life was given in hours; the printed answer 14.44 omits the unit and differs only in the fourth figure, from rounding of the logarithm.)

Given: \(N_0 = 0.5\) g, \(N = 0.0788\) g, \(t = 8\) days. (Masses may be used in place of numbers of nuclei, since the two are proportional for one isotope.)

**Step 1 — decay constant.**

\(\lambda = \dfrac{2.303}{t}\ \log_{10}\dfrac{N_0}{N} = \dfrac{2.303}{8\ \mathrm{d}}\ \log_{10}\dfrac{0.5}{0.0788}\)

\(= 0.28788\ \mathrm{d^{-1}} \times \log_{10}(6.345) = 0.28788\ \mathrm{d^{-1}} \times 0.80252 = 0.2310\ \mathrm{d^{-1}}\)

**Step 2 — half life.**

\(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{\lambda} = \dfrac{0.693}{0.2310\ \mathrm{d^{-1}}} = 3.0\ \mathrm{d}\)

**The half life of \(^{201}\mathrm{Tl}\) is 3.0 days.**

(Check: 8 days is close to \(2\tfrac{2}{3}\) half lives, and \(0.5/2^{8/3} = 0.0787\) g, which is the mass given.)

Given: 65 % of the sample decays in 4.2 d, so 35 % remains. Take \(N_0 = 100\), \(N = 35\), \(t = 4.2\) d.

**Step 1 — decay constant.**

\(\lambda = \dfrac{2.303}{t}\ \log_{10}\dfrac{N_0}{N} = \dfrac{2.303}{4.2\ \mathrm{d}}\ \log_{10}\dfrac{100}{35}\)

\(= 0.54833\ \mathrm{d^{-1}} \times \log_{10}(2.857) = 0.54833\ \mathrm{d^{-1}} \times 0.45593 = 0.2500\ \mathrm{d^{-1}}\)

**Step 2 — half life.**

\(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{\lambda} = \dfrac{0.693}{0.2500\ \mathrm{d^{-1}}} = 2.77\ \mathrm{d}\)

For \(^{84}_{36}\mathrm{Kr}\): \(Z = 36\), \(A = 84\), so \(A - Z = 48\) neutrons. \(m = 83.913\) u.

**Step 1 — mass defect,** using Eq. (13.2), \(\Delta m = [Z m_{\mathrm{H}} + (A - Z) m_{\mathrm{n}}] - m\):

\(\Delta m = [36 \times 1.0078\ \mathrm{u} + 48 \times 1.0087\ \mathrm{u}] - 83.913\ \mathrm{u}\)

\(= [36.2808 + 48.4176]\ \mathrm{u} - 83.913\ \mathrm{u} = 84.6984\ \mathrm{u} - 83.913\ \mathrm{u} = 0.7854\ \mathrm{u}\)

**Step 2 — total binding energy,** using Eq. (13.3):

\(\mathrm{B.E.} = \Delta m\ (\mathrm{u}) \times 931.4 = 0.7854 \times 931.4 = 731.5\ \mathrm{MeV}\)

**Step 3 — binding energy per nucleon,** using Eq. (13.4):

\(\overline{B} = \dfrac{\mathrm{B.E.}}{A} = \dfrac{731.5\ \mathrm{MeV}}{84} = 8.71\ \mathrm{MeV\ per\ nucleon}\)

**The binding energy per nucleon of \(^{84}\mathrm{Kr}\) is about 8.7 MeV.**

**Step 1 — mass defect of the reaction.** The energy released comes from the mass lost in going from reactant to products:

\(\Delta m = \text{mass of } ^{174}\mathrm{Ir} - (\text{mass of } ^{170}\mathrm{Re} + \text{mass of } ^{4}\mathrm{He})\)

\(= 173.97\ \mathrm{u} - (169.96\ \mathrm{u} + 4.0026\ \mathrm{u})\)

\(= 173.97\ \mathrm{u} - 173.9626\ \mathrm{u} = 0.0074\ \mathrm{u}\)

**Step 2 — convert the mass loss to energy,** using \(1\ \mathrm{u} \equiv 931.4\) MeV:

\(E = \Delta m\ (\mathrm{u}) \times 931.4 = 0.0074 \times 931.4 = 6.89\ \mathrm{MeV}\)

**The energy released in the reaction is 6.89 MeV.**

(\(\Delta m\) is positive, so mass is lost and energy is RELEASED, as it must be for a spontaneous \(\alpha\)-decay.)

If \(3/4\) of the original amount has decayed, then the amount REMAINING is

\(1 - \dfrac{3}{4} = \dfrac{1}{4}\) of the original.

By the definition of half life, each half life halves the amount remaining:

\(N_0 \xrightarrow{\ t_{1/2}\ } \dfrac{N_0}{2} \xrightarrow{\ t_{1/2}\ } \dfrac{N_0}{4}\)

So reaching one quarter takes **two** half lives, and those two half lives occupy 60 minutes:

\(2\ t_{1/2} = 60\ \mathrm{min}\), hence \(t_{1/2} = 30\ \mathrm{min}\)

**The half life of the radioisotope is 30 minutes.**

(The same result follows from the rate law: \(\lambda = \dfrac{2.303}{60\ \mathrm{min}}\log_{10} 4 = 0.0231\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}\), and \(t_{1/2} = 0.693/0.0231 = 30\) min.)

[Textbook misprint / answer-key error, two places. (i) The stem reads "How many - particles", with the particle symbol missing before the hyphen; radium-226 is an \(\alpha\)-emitter (section 13.6.1), so these are \(\alpha\)-particles. (ii) The stem gives no half life, and the printed answer \(1.154 \times 10^{17}\) is what \(t_{1/2} = 1600\) y would give — but the only half life this chapter supplies for radium-226 is 1620 y, in Table 13.4 (b), and that gives \(1.14 \times 10^{17}\). The printed answer therefore contradicts the chapter's own table.]

The number of particles emitted in a given time is the **activity** of the sample, \(-\dfrac{dN}{dt} = \lambda N\). Radium-226 is an \(\alpha\)-emitter — section 13.6.1 gives its decay as \(^{226}_{88}\mathrm{Ra} \longrightarrow {}^{222}_{86}\mathrm{Rn} + {}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}\) — so the particles counted are \(\alpha\)-particles.

**Step 1 — decay constant.** The stem does not give the half life; Table 13.4 (b) of this chapter gives \(t_{1/2} = 1620\) y for radium-226.

\(\lambda = \dfrac{0.693}{1620\ \mathrm{y}} = 4.278 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{y^{-1}}\)

**Step 2 — number of nuclei in 0.1 g.**

\(N = \dfrac{0.1\ \mathrm{g}}{226\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23}\ \mathrm{mol^{-1}} = 2.665 \times 10^{20}\) nuclei

**Step 3 — activity.**

\(-\dfrac{dN}{dt} = \lambda N = 4.278 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{y^{-1}} \times 2.665 \times 10^{20} = 1.14 \times 10^{17}\ \mathrm{y^{-1}}\)

**About \(1.14 \times 10^{17}\) \(\alpha\)-particles are emitted in one year.**

**Step 1 — put both activities in the same unit.** Section 13.5.6 gives \(1\ \mathrm{Ci} = 3.7 \times 10^{10}\) dps, so the initial activity is

\(-\dfrac{dN_0}{dt} = 3.7 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{dps}\), and after 303 days \(-\dfrac{dN}{dt} = 1.5 \times 10^{4}\ \mathrm{dps}\).

Since activity is proportional to the number of nuclei, the ratio of activities equals \(N_0/N\).

**Step 2 — decay constant.**

\(\lambda = \dfrac{2.303}{t}\ \log_{10}\dfrac{N_0}{N} = \dfrac{2.303}{303\ \mathrm{d}}\ \log_{10}\dfrac{3.7 \times 10^{10}}{1.5 \times 10^{4}}\)

\(= 7.601 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{d^{-1}} \times \log_{10}(2.467 \times 10^{6})\)

\(= 7.601 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{d^{-1}} \times 6.392 = 0.04858\ \mathrm{d^{-1}}\)

**Step 3 — half life.**

\(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{\lambda} = \dfrac{0.693}{0.04858\ \mathrm{d^{-1}}} = 14.27\ \mathrm{d}\)

**The half life of \(^{32}\mathrm{P}\) is 14.27 days.**

Given: \(t_{1/2} = 3.82\) d. If 99.9 % has decayed, 0.1 % remains: take \(N_0 = 100\) and \(N = 100 - 99.9 = 0.1\).

**Step 1 — decay constant.**

\(\lambda = \dfrac{0.693}{3.82\ \mathrm{d}} = 0.18141\ \mathrm{d^{-1}}\)

**Step 2 — time required.**

\(t = \dfrac{2.303}{\lambda}\ \log_{10}\dfrac{N_0}{N} = \dfrac{2.303}{0.18141\ \mathrm{d^{-1}}}\ \log_{10}\dfrac{100}{0.1}\)

\(= 12.695\ \mathrm{d} \times \log_{10}(1000) = 12.695\ \mathrm{d} \times 3 = 38.1\ \mathrm{d}\)

**Radon will be 99.9 % decayed after about 38.1 days**, that is roughly 10 half lives (\(2^{10} = 1024 \approx 1000\)).

The Sun radiates energy because it loses mass, and the two are connected by Einstein's equation \(E = mc^{2}\) (section 13.3.5).

Given: \(m = 4.34 \times 10^{9}\) kg lost per second, \(c = 3 \times 10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\ s^{-1}}\).

\(E = mc^{2} = 4.34 \times 10^{9}\ \mathrm{kg} \times (3 \times 10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\ s^{-1}})^{2}\)

\(= 4.34 \times 10^{9} \times 9 \times 10^{16}\ \mathrm{J}\)

\(= 3.906 \times 10^{26}\ \mathrm{J}\)

Converting to kilojoules,

\(E = \dfrac{3.906 \times 10^{26}}{10^{3}}\ \mathrm{kJ} = 3.9 \times 10^{23}\ \mathrm{kJ}\)

**The Sun radiates about \(3.9 \times 10^{23}\) kJ into space every second**, that is \(3.9 \times 10^{23}\ \mathrm{kJ\ s^{-1}}\). This energy is the result of the nuclear fusion reactions taking place in the Sun.

[Textbook misprint: the printed answer is given as "6833 g". The question asks for the AGE of the wood sample, so the unit is years, not grams. The value 6833 is correct.]

This is radiocarbon dating (section 13.8.1). The fresh sample gives the activity the wood had at the moment the tree died, so \(N_0 = 16.0\) dps/g and \(N = 7.0\) dps/g.

**Step 1 — decay constant of \(^{14}\mathrm{C}\).**

\(\lambda = \dfrac{0.693}{5730\ \mathrm{y}} = 1.21 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{y^{-1}}\)

**Step 2 — age of the sample.**

\(t = \dfrac{2.303}{\lambda}\ \log_{10}\dfrac{N_0}{N} = \dfrac{2.303}{1.21 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{y^{-1}}}\ \log_{10}\dfrac{16.0}{7.0}\)

\(= 1.9033 \times 10^{4}\ \mathrm{y} \times \log_{10}(2.2857)\)

\(= 1.9033 \times 10^{4}\ \mathrm{y} \times 0.35908 = 6833\ \mathrm{y}\)

**The wood sample is about 6833 years old.**

(The answer is an age, so the unit is YEARS; the chapter's own rounded value \(\lambda = 1.21 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{y^{-1}}\) has been used, and carrying \(0.693/5730\) unrounded gives 6837 y.)
